# Agentic Pipeline Report: 20 Newsgroups (4 categories)

*I loaded four newsgroup categories with `load_dataset_tool` (`load_dataset_1`): 2,257 documents in total, split into soc.religion.christian (599), sci.med (594), comp.graphics (584) and alt.atheism (480). These are the same categories as the Master notebook, so the numbers were able to be compared directly. Looking at the first rows (`inspect_data_2`) showed that every post still begins with its email headers (From, Subject, Organization), which turned out to matter for almost every later step. The missing-text check (`check_missing_3`) and the duplicate check (`check_duplicates_4`) both found 0 missing or duplicates, so no rows were removed. I skipped sampling on purpose to keep the full dataset comparable with Master. The length box plot (`describe_data_5`) shows that typical posts in all four categories are short (a few thousand characters at most), but every category has long outliers. The most extreme are four comp.graphics posts between about 47,000 and 61,000 characters and one alt.atheism post of about 51,000.*

![Document text length by category](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_describe_data_5.png)

*Next, I built the document-term matrix with `build_dtm_tool` using the default settings (`dtm_6`). It has 2,257 rows and 35,788 terms, which matches Master, and it is 99.547% sparse. A typical post uses only about 162 distinct words. The heatmap of the first 20 terms and documents (`dtm_heatmap_8`) shows that the first terms alphabetically are number strings, and only 2 of its 400 cells are non-zero. I then ran `variance_filter_tool` with a threshold of 0.01, first only to count (`variance_filter_9`) and then removing terms (`variance_filter_10`). This removed 30,434 terms (85%), mostly rare tokens like numbers and usernames, and kept 5,354 of them. The trade-off is that rare but category-specific words can be lost as well.*

![DTM heatmap](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_dtm_heatmap_8.png)

*The correlation filters showed how strongly this raw text is shaped by content that is not about the topic. In `pearson_filter_11` for sci.med, only about 4 of the top 20 terms are medical (medicine, treatment, sensitivity, diet). About 12 come from one frequent poster's name, email address and signature quote (gordon, banks, geb, n3jxp, cadre, dsl, pitt, plus skepticism, chastity, intellect, shameful, surrender). The quote words have nearly identical r values because they almost always appear together. `spearman_filter_12` brings up more real medical words (disease, medical, doctor, health, patients) and gives "god" a negative r, meaning it signals a post is not sci.med, but the signature words are still at the top. The lists differ because Pearson works on raw counts, so a few posts that repeat a word many times can pull it up, while Spearman works on ranks. The same kind of problem appeared twice more. The 20 highest-variance terms in `feature_correlation_matrix_tool` (`feature_corr_13`) are mostly stopwords plus "edu" and "jpeg", and they correlate strongly with each other ("the" and "of": 0.94) because longer posts contain more of every common word, not because of meaning. Pattern mining with `mine_patterns_tool` (`patterns_14`: sci.med, tfidf, fpgrowth, min_sup 80, the same as Master) found 8,495 patterns, but the top ones are header fields such as "subject" (in all 594 posts), "lines", "organization", "edu", "writes" and "article". The huge number comes from every combination of these near-universal words, and since every category has them, they cannot separate categories.*

![Top Pearson terms for sci.med](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_turn94.png)
![Top-variance term correlation matrix](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_feature_corr_13.png)

*I then reduced the DTM to 2 dimensions with `reduce_dimensions_tool`. With PCA (`reduction_15`), PC1 explains 67.2% of the variance and PC2 only 4.4%. In the plot, almost all posts are squeezed into one blob with the categories mixed together, while a few points lie far out along PC1: four comp.graphics posts and one alt.atheism post. These match the extreme outliers in the length box plot, so PC1 mostly measures post length, not topic. UMAP (`reduction_16`) separates the categories better: there is a distinct alt.atheism cluster at the bottom, a sci.med cluster at the bottom left, and comp.graphics gathers on the right side. Soc.religion.christian is spread across the left and overlaps with alt.atheism, which makes sense because both discuss God, belief and the Bible. Still, most posts remain mixed, likely because stopwords and headers make all posts look alike.*

![PCA](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_reduction_15.png)
![UMAP](../plots/Emily_On_agentic-pipeline_plot_reduction_16.png)

*Lastly, I one-hot encoded the category labels with `binarize_labels_tool` (`binarize_17`), which produced a 2,257 x 4 table of 0s and 1s with one column per category. The counts (480, 584, 594, 599) match what I loaded, so nothing was lost. To test whether posts from the same category are more alike, I compared one same-category pair and one different-category pair with `cosine_similarity_tool`. Two soc.religion.christian posts (documents 2 and 3, `cosine_sim_18`) scored 0.3016, while a comp.graphics and a soc.religion.christian post (documents 0 and 2, `cosine_sim_19`) scored 0.3399. The different-category pair scored higher because cosine compares raw word counts, and the largest counts are stopwords and header words that every post shares, although with only two pairs this is an example rather than proof. In conclusion, the same problem appeared in four different methods: a poster's signature in the correlation filters, stopwords in the feature correlation, header fields in pattern mining, and shared filler words in cosine similarity. On raw newsgroup text, these methods mostly capture who wrote a post and how emails are formatted rather than what the post is about. The next step would be to strip headers and signatures and remove stopwords before filtering, then rerun the pipeline.*
